Tinker Taylor Founder Guy: Q&A with Bret Taylor - Colossus

# Tinker Taylor Founder Guy 

 A conversation with Bret Taylor, who has achieved nearly every feat in business except the one he says matters most 

 By Dom Cooke 

 November 2026 

 ![](https://colossus.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/NateKitch-Collossus-Bret-Taylor-Final-Digital-alt-photo-scaled.jpg) 

 ILLUSTRATION BY NATE KITCH¹ 

In our joyless era of orthorexia, there are precious few tech figures left who pass the beer test. The basic exam to which American voters subject their candidates for office, the beer test is a simple evaluation of tastes and nature: Is this person willing and able to drink a beer? Would I enjoy their company while they do it? Can they drink without going on a podcast to explain that it wrecked their sleep and productivity? If so, they pass the beer test, which I find still tells you more about a person than can be gleaned from their pitch deck, S-1, or whatever product they’ve recently commissioned a video about on X.

I was recently surprised to find that Bret Taylor passes this cloudy yet robust benchmark. It helps that Taylor is one of the few who still drinks, but the attribute most in his favor is that he is simply normal. In the course of my work, I’m often told that such-and-such founder has both high IQ and high EQ. It is meant as a signal that the person is normal. It is, in fact, a reliable sign they are not. No one says this about Bret Taylor. They just say, “He is normal.”

Then they wonder aloud, how? How could the man who created Google Maps; invented the Like button; sold his first startup to Facebook for $50 million; became Facebook’s chief technology officer in his twenties; sold his next startup to Salesforce for $750 million; was chairman of Twitter when Elon Musk bought it, and sued Musk when he tried to back out; became co-CEO of Salesforce; bought a piece of the San Francisco 49ers; and is now the chairman of OpenAI—how could that person be normal?

I am British, and therefore no psychologist. But if I ventured an answer, I might mention Taylor’s father, Steven, who ran a heating and ventilation firm in Alameda, California, and to this day calls his son for help when he gets lost using Google Maps. Or I might mention his mother, Sheila, who was a vice president of marketing at Chevron before starting a wine country tour business; Taylor doubts she knows what Salesforce does, though he spent six and a half years there. Or I might mention his sister, who he is close to, and who has a real job. She is a public school teacher.

There are also his setbacks, which seem proportional to his achievements, and may have helped keep him planted. At Facebook, he was, by his own admission, responsible for what Mark Zuckerberg described in 2012 as the biggest mistake the company had ever made: Rather than write its mobile app specifically for the iPhone and Android, Facebook built it in HTML5 (the code used to make websites). The Facebook app got a rating of one and a half stars, and Zuckerberg said it cost the company two years.

At Salesforce, it was clear to everyone that Taylor was Benioff’s heir, until November 2021, when Benioff instead made him co-chief executive, sharing the job rather than handing it over. A year later, Taylor announced he was leaving. Benioff, who initially gushed about the $28 billion Slack acquisition Taylor had orchestrated, distanced himself from it. When The Information asked Benioff about his former protégé’s new company, Sierra, he replied by text: “Sorry, I don’t know anything about them.”

The point is not to psychoanalyze Taylor, however; that is for his wife to sort out. What interests me is that he embodies a paradox. He is both normal and a successful tech leader, which is to say he is not supposed to exist. It figures, then, that his career grew out of a few happy accidents.

For his 16th birthday, when Taylor still dressed like a punk rocker and wore long, greasy hair, he bought a used 1971 Volkswagen bus. On the day he got his license, he was parking at a movie theater in Walnut Creek, a town in the East Bay, when he scratched a brand-new Cadillac. He left a note. The Cadillac’s owner, who ran a gas station, called and offered him a summer job to pay for the repair. Taylor pumped gas and cleaned the station’s toilets for $4.25 an hour, in a shirt that said “Brent.” 

When a mechanic next door grumbled about the cost of building a website, Taylor asked how much he’d pay someone to do it. “$400,” the mechanic said. So Taylor went to a computer lab at a community college, learned how to make websites, got paid $400, quit the gas station, and went door-to-door in Lafayette, signing up customers to his new internet business. Still, what he really wanted was to become a lawyer. Stanford, where he ended up only because his sister was there, soon beat that out of him. Then, in 2003, he practically flipped a coin to pick between offers from Google and VMware.

It is a near certainty that the VMware version of Taylor wouldn’t have received a call from OpenAI 20 years later, in November 2023. At the time, the company had created the most viral consumer product in history and was on its way to an $86 billion valuation when, on a Friday, its board of directors decided to blow it up. They fired the CEO, removed the chairman, and watched as nine in 10 employees threatened to quit, while Microsoft, its biggest investor, hired the man they had fired.

Taylor, who had no stake in the company beyond a growing emotional attachment to ChatGPT, learned of this “blip” on social media, like the rest of us. Unlike the rest of us, he was perhaps the only person with the requisite skills and experience to pick up the pieces.

OpenAI was on course to become the defining consumer business of its generation. Taylor had worked at the two before it, Google and Facebook. It needed a grown-up who could handle politicians and prima donnas. Taylor had testified before the United States Senate multiple times, sat on boards in peacetime, at Axon and Shopify, and chaired one in wartime, at Twitter. OpenAI was a research lab, and Taylor was, at heart, still a software engineer. 

So it was Taylor the board called. He had once been asked about joining OpenAI’s board and said no. “I was never going to do a board again,” he recalls. His wife asked whether, on his deathbed, he would regret not helping. “Whose side are you on, honey?” he replied. Within days, he was chairman.

All of which brings me back to the paradox, and the reason I wanted to call on Taylor. He has done almost everything a person can do in business. But there is one feat he has yet to accomplish, and it is the one he thinks matters most. “I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

The products Taylor has created have had a lasting impact on society. Google Maps is ubiquitous. His first startup, FriendFeed, is often credited with inventing the Like button and pioneering real-time social feeds. But his companies have not endured. Both FriendFeed and Quip were acquired and then shut down by Facebook and Salesforce, respectively. The deals were as much about the people as the products. Inside Salesforce, some called Taylor “the 750-million-dollar man.”

Perhaps, then, there is no paradox. A normal person can build incredible products, run other people’s companies, even rescue them from catastrophe. But building a generational company, the kind that goes public and mints billions of dollars, maybe that’s for the crazy ones only. 

I hope not, and Taylor has another chance to prove it isn’t. In 2023, he co-founded his third company, Sierra, with his long-time friend Clay Bavor. Unlike Taylor, Bavor stayed at Google for more than 18 years and became one of its most senior executives, reporting to CEO Sundar Pichai. Taylor tried to recruit him to every company he joined or started. Bavor always said no. Then, in late 2022, just as ChatGPT launched, Taylor announced he was leaving Salesforce, and the two sat down for a long lunch. They resolved to start an AI company together. What it would do, they hadn’t yet decided.

By March, they settled on building AI agents for large businesses to talk to their customers. When I first heard Taylor was applying AI to customer service, it seemed beneath him. It was, after all, the most obvious place to put AI. But with the arrival of personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and Dots in the past few months, it has become clear that the era of the website and the app is likely ending. 

If it is, the agent a company puts in front of its customers effectively becomes the company, not just its support line. Say you call your car insurer with a benign question, like “When is my policy up for renewal?” An agent will respond, and remind you when the time comes. But it also knows your file and is incapable of sloth. So it might point out that your son will be old enough to drive soon, and it could add him to your policy, or that your home would be cheaper insured in the same place, and look, there’s a deal for your wife too, wouldn’t you like to save some more money? 

When a human tries to have these conversations with you, it is unbearable. It’s worse than talking to Alexa, who has been stripped of her responsibilities bar turning my lights on and off, and she’s on her final warning there. But frontier AI models are genuinely impressive, so I hold hope that conversing with AI agents may be tolerable. And perhaps I’ll never have to talk to a company agent because my personal agent will take care of it, interrupting me only when it absolutely has to. Taylor showed me a video of Muse doing more or less that, filling out a mortgage application with Rocket Mortgage’s agent, which Sierra built. Or maybe it all makes for a great demo but never works as advertised, which I put to Taylor after reckoning with their AI agent for Sonos, twice.

Investors, at least, believe in Sierra’s vision. A new funding round has valued the startup at more than $30 billion, making it the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own. Whether he can keep Sierra out of the clutches of, oh, I don’t know, OpenAI, remains to be seen. But it’s clear that Taylor, who was there for the web, for social media, for the smartphone, and for the cloud, will be in the room deciding how the most important economic relationship there is—the one between a business and its customer—gets reinvented by AI. I’m reassured someone normal will be there.

With all this bubbling away in my head, I strode through Sierra’s office in San Francisco, past a copy of Will Guidara’s Unreasonable Hospitality, dozens of workers dressed in denim, and an eleven-and-a-half-foot alphorn hanging on the wall—blown by employees whenever a new customer is signed—to meet with Taylor, who was waiting for me in a nondescript conference room. 

What follows is a transcript of our conversation. It has been lightly edited and condensed for your reading pleasure. No beers were consumed, but only because it was 9am.

Dom Cooke: I’ve just been told that you all wear denim on the last Thursday of every quarter, but no one seems to know why. Do you?

Bret Taylor: I don’t, actually. But let me look. 

Have you seen Pinecone? It’s pretty amazing.

I haven’t.

It’s an internal agent. We run everything on it. You chat with it, you write code with it. I’ll show you the results. [Starts typing] “What’s the backstory detail of Double Denim?”

It’s double denim?

Yeah, you gotta do both.

I’m pretty sure Logan Randolph, who was one of our early employees, and Natasha, who runs operations here, came up with it. And then it’s sort of stupid so people latch onto it.

There’s literally a schedule now. People always worry I’ll forget because I’m absent-minded. Look at the text message from my assistant at 6am, “Denim day!!!” I got like five text messages this morning, “Don’t forget to wear denim!” 

[Looking at his shirt] I think this might be linen, but it looks like denim.

It looks denim to me.

[Showing me his laptop] This is the timeline from our AI agent: “So, we couldn’t find a public Slack mention, but apparently August 5th 2024 it was announced with the words, “This is not a joke.”

So not only are you celebrating denim for a reason none of you remember. But, today, you’re also announcing that you added $150 million in annual recurring revenue in the last three months, which is more than all of last year. How do you reflect on that?

Well, first, it’s pretty neat. Essentially I’ve started three companies and, I guess normally you wouldn’t put it this way, but the other two didn’t succeed independently, right? And so when you sell your company, people always congratulate you. But as an entrepreneur, you can’t say how you actually feel because you just got a bunch of money.

You’ll seem ungrateful. 

Yeah. No one starts a company thinking, “I want to sell it.” You start a company thinking you want to make the next Google or Facebook or Microsoft. 

So what’s really neat is that it feels like we’ve made a company that is reaching escape velocity. Maybe it has already reached it, though everything in AI is so tumultuous I don’t think you can use the past tense. I’m really proud of it. It’s really fun. Clay and I just pinch ourselves every day.

What’s most fulfilling is, I actually don’t know where I’d stack up age-wise, but I’m older for an entrepreneur. And I think in our industry experience has been an asset, because we’re on the bleeding edge of technology, but a storied bank will return our calls. We have a unique market position. I guess every entrepreneur says this, but I think we have the best product. We also have a brand and a reputation for being able to engage with more traditional companies, and that’s really differentiated right now.

Often you have to choose. Do you go with a company whose tech is good, even though it might not exist in two years? Or do you buy from an incumbent, knowing the technology is bad but that you can procure from them sustainably? We’ve hit this really unique value proposition where we offer both, and I’m really proud of it.

Did you ever get to a point with Quip where you felt like you had this but then lost it, or you actually never felt like you got to this point?

I had two really different experiences with FriendFeed and Quip. With FriendFeed, we felt it and lost it. The company only lasted like a year.

I was surprised how short it was.

It was a flash in the pan. But at one point we were on the cover of BusinessWeek magazine, or had some spread. It was a big deal for us at the time. We were the hot “it” company for about a month, and then we got our butts kicked, primarily by Twitter.

Maybe this has been embellished through the lens of time, but I remember Oprah and Ashton Kutcher and Obama getting on Twitter. Social networking is a network-effect business, so there isn’t really a silver medal for second place. We went from “We’re amazing” to “We’ve clearly lost.” It felt quite definitive to me.

We ran a sale process. We did a redesign. It was the dead cat bounce kind of thing. Then we debated. We only had 12 people. We could have run FriendFeed for a very long time because we were so efficient. But we talked about it and decided to make it known through back channels that we might be on the market. We ended up with a fairly competitive process because, despite not winning, we were known to be innovative. It was a competitive talent acquisition is the way I’d put it.

> I’ve started three companies and, I guess normally you wouldn’t put it this way, but the other two didn’t succeed independently, right? And so when you sell your company, people always congratulate you. But as an entrepreneur, you can’t say how you actually feel because you just got a bunch of money.

Quip was a good product. We had happy customers. It just wasn’t as big as I think it could have been. We might have been able to stay independent and go public. But, and this is going to sound funny, being a $2 billion, $3 billion or $4 billion market cap tech company is a tough place to be. It’s hard to attract talent, and you don’t really have the currency to do acquisitions.

So when we were growing at a pace that was fine but not like this [drawing a steep line in the air], you have to make a choice. Do you want to be in it for the long term, recognizing that it’s a different thing? When we started Quip, we really felt the addressable market was Microsoft Office. But when you’re growing like this [drawing a flatter line in the air], you’re like, okay, well, we’re clearly not addressing that market. To be overly blunt, we had made a niche product. 

Selling Quip was tougher because we definitely didn’t have to. With FriendFeed, we lost. With Quip, the stars aligned and a strategic acquirer came along. We were grown-ups about it.

No one expected you to stay at Salesforce for six and a half years. It ended up being your longest tenure to date. Why is that? 

When I got to Salesforce, I thought I was going to be there for about three years. I felt very grateful to the company for acquiring us, and it was done at a premium. I don’t know how to itemize the receipt, but I thought part of it was: Quip is fine, but come here and contribute. So I had this mentality of, “Whatever Marc asks me to do, I’m going to do.”

After a year or so, the previous chief product officer, Alex Dayon, wanted to move to a different role. Marc asked me to take over. It was a much more central casting role, not like go do a special project kind of thing, which is what I had—

Envisioned.

Yeah, and I felt uncomfortable about it. I didn’t feel qualified in some ways to do it, and that’s not feigned humility. It was just a big company with a lot of history. I didn’t completely understand the entire product portfolio and it felt like one of those jobs you should grow up to do. I had imposter syndrome but I felt gratitude to Salesforce and to Marc, and so I didn’t feel entitled to say no. I just said, “Great, I’m going to work hard at it.” 

Then you grow attached to the place. I got fulfillment from making products that I was proud of and driving results I was proud of. And I really enjoyed being mentored by Marc, who’s a very different type of person than I am. I learned a lot from him just because we have such different DNA.

Then the pandemic happened, and I don’t think I was alone in this, but the focus was on keeping the thing on the rails. We had something like 50,000 or 60,000 people at the beginning of the pandemic, you’re just like—

Let’s look after it.

Then you look up and think, “Wow, I’ve been here for a long time.” But I have no regrets. I really enjoyed the place and I still feel a lot of affinity for it.

 ![](https://colossus.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-1243391612-scaled.jpg) 

Photo by Bloomberg via Getty Images

Taylor and Marc Benioff hosting Salesforce’s 2022 Dreamforce conference.

After you left Salesforce, I saw a picture of a whiteboard you put up in your house. You and Clay had decided to start a business. On the board, under the title “MASTER PLAN”, you’d written, “1: Quit our jobs.” Step two was just a series of question marks. How did you end up coalescing on the idea behind Sierra?

For the first few weeks, Clay and I were just brainstorming about the capabilities of the frontier models and having first principles discussions about, “Okay, then what?” “Okay, then what?” We were going through our theories of the world.

I don’t remember which of us had the idea, but we decided to email some leaders at businesses we had relationships with from our past jobs. Basically, people who would accept our calls.

Probably the most important was a call with Anthony Tan, the CEO of Grab. I don’t think this is too embellished. I think it was as significant as I remember. It was very late because he’s based in Singapore. I remember it being around 9pm. This was probably our 10th or 11th call, and we were just asking these folks, “You’ve got two founders here. If you could wave a wand and have us work on one problem, selfishly, just for you, what would it be?”

Fun question.

Anthony was emphatic about customer service. If you know the delivery and ridesharing business, and particularly one that operates in multiple countries with multiple languages, it’s just a really complex operation. You have to provide 24/7 service in Singlish, Tamil, Malay, Tagalog, and all the other markets he serves. 

He gave me the first principles view about why we should work in this area. We had heard similar things from other people, but we hadn’t heard it quite so crisply. Then Clay and I started talking to other companies saying, “If we were to work in this area, how would it impact your business?”

But one of the main things we discussed before deciding to start Sierra was where it would take us. Amazon started as a bookseller and ended up as something much greater. So the question was: If we start here, what adjacent areas would it give us permission to work in, and are they interesting to us?

We came to the concept of the digital front door fairly quickly. The hypothesis was that you might call a company with a customer service inquiry, but that experience will probably expand to do everything over time, the same way websites did. That became really exciting for us. It had the unique quality of being a compelling short-term opportunity and a really expansive long-term one. When you’re trying to make an enduring company, you really want to care about both.

In all three businesses you’ve started, your co-founders have come from Google. Was the talent density there just so off the charts? Is there some romanticism about Google because it was your first job? Or, is it pure coincidence?

That’s really interesting. I hadn’t realized that until right now. Certainly very high talent density. Google was my first job out of university, and I made a lot of close friends there. I met my wife there. And so it’s a little bit like why a lot of people are close to their university friends. It’s a time in your life where you form very deep connections. I’ve truly known Clay since 2004. It’s been a long time.

Sarah Guo told me a story about Quip. To hire the early team, she said you put offer letters under people’s chairs at a dinner. Tell me that story.

It’s slightly embellished, but true. A gentleman named Mike Cassidy, who had started a few different businesses, became my trusted advisor as an entrepreneur. When we were first raising money for FriendFeed, I would ask him to define terms for me. Just the basics. This is before Y Combinator and all that when there were no cheat codes.

One of his main pieces of advice—in fact, he has this whole spiel about it—was about how important speed is for startups. Moving fast is one of the few things that you can reliably do better than incumbents. So his philosophy was that everything you do, you should try to do extremely quickly, or ask, “Why can’t it be faster?”

One of the areas where we really adopted his advice was hiring. If you know the person you’re talking to, maybe it’s a colleague you’ve worked with before or whatever, there isn’t much to learn. So have a meal with them and give them an offer letter. Don’t wait, and don’t go through some elaborate process. Emotionally, candidates really feel it. That’s how we hired our first 10 people at Quip.

Did you do anything similar at Sierra?

Definitely. In fact, Mihai Parparita, who was our first hire, had worked at Quip. He got the dinner experience there, and again here. For the first few people, we did something very similar. It’s effective.

Noah Shinn, founder of Instinct, was one of the first people to work at Sierra. He dropped out of college to join. How did you find him? It’s interesting now that you’re both building agents, one for people, the other for businesses.

This is a funny story. We were reading a lot of research papers. Most were on arXiv rather than in journals, because there was such a proliferation of papers when we started. We found one called “Reflexion.” It was about a technique where you have an LLM review, or reflect on, its results, and you reliably get better outcomes. It was a simple technique, but they showed scientifically how much more effective it could make reasoning and adherence.

It was one of those really clever things, and very much in the wheelhouse of what an applied AI company like Sierra needs to do all day from a research perspective. So I cold-emailed him. I assumed he was a grad student at Northeastern, because I think he had two papers on arXiv. He gets on the Zoom, and let’s just say he looked his age. I was like, “Oh my God.” I think I just asked him, “How old are you?” He was a freshman. And in my head, I’m thinking, “Man, when I was a freshman, I was just trying to find a party.”

Me and you both.

So on the call, I asked if he’d be interested in an internship. I think he’d been considering an internship at one of the labs, maybe OpenAI, but he was very interested in applied AI. Within a week or so, he agreed and showed up, which was awesome. It was intended to be an internship, but he never went back and we made him a full-time employee. 

Eventually he decided to start what became Instinct. People like Noah are truly remarkable. I wasn’t joking before. Freshman year, I would have been happy to find the cafeteria. And he’s publishing research papers. It’s pretty amazing.

You went to Stanford and studied computer science. But when you first got there, you wanted to be a lawyer?

Yes. I was on the mock trial team, and I had gone to the summer program at Brown and taken a constitutional law class. It just felt like a real job. But when I arrived at Stanford in 1998, the bubble was bigger, or at least as big, as this one. So my law dreams lasted about 10 minutes. I knew I liked programming, I just didn’t know it could be a career. 

I feel really lucky that I was at Stanford. I wonder how it would have been different if I’d been on the East Coast. I don’t know. But Stanford in 1998, you were in the dot-com bubble. I didn’t have to pay for dinner because there were all these companies recruiting everywhere handing out free pizza. You just feigned interest in their company and got free food. It was just part of the culture. Would I have ended up in finance or something? I have no idea. I just totally lucked out.

What were you really into as a kid?

I’m going to embarrass myself here. I was very into punk rock. There was an article that came out during the Twitter saga, and they found an old photo of me with long hair. It was mortifying.

 ![](https://colossus.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/4c93b33448d4b7feb767ac45a5f4b69e2d7a51a0-2.png) 

PHOTO BY ANCESTRY

Taylor, aged 16, pictured in his Acalanes High School yearbook.

I was always a good student, but a little rebellious. I had a band, and I loved music. It was that era. When did Nirvana’s Nevermind come out?

I have no idea.

That captured me.

There’s a club in Berkeley called Gilman Street. It was an all-ages club where a lot of punk bands played. That was my scene. Then my good friend ended up in a ska band, and I’d roadie for them so we could get into clubs before we were of age to get into clubs and stuff like that.

 ![](https://colossus.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Stanford-Show.jpeg) 

Taylor (far right) playing in the punk band he formed with applied physics PhD students in college. He still has that guitar at home.

Do you think we’ll ever get back to 2012–13 Bret who was tweeting about football all the time?

I wish I could. The problem with social media right now is it’s gotten very big. I loved that era.

You have to think too hard now when you tweet something.

That’s right. I also find open source projects less fun now because people know who I am. I can’t just dive into a community. So I do have a sense of loss there. I have strong opinions.

It’s always struck me as bizarre how influential X is in the tech community. It seems like lots of people who run big businesses, particularly in this part of the world, spend a lot of their time on X, either getting product ideas or talking to other folks. Does that strike you as weird or normal?

I think the service is really interesting. There was always something about early tech where we embraced bulletin boards, before even HTTP. I think the best form of it is truth-seeking, or science, where people share notes on things. It’s why in public forums and open source there’s a strong thread of, “We’re collectively moving the status quo forward and innovating together.” The downside is you get flame wars and toxicity and everything else. Unfortunately those two things are like strands of intertwined DNA.

But it doesn’t surprise me for that reason. There’s a through line from the early bulletin board systems to this. A communal sense that’s always been part of tech, from arguing about tabs versus spaces to now arguing about the economics of token consumption. It’s everything you think it is. Both mildly annoying and kind of endearing.

Yeah, that’s why people can’t get rid of it.

Exactly.

When you sold Quip, I read that you brought two kegs into the office. The question is: How do we make drinking cool again? In moderation, obviously.

[Laughing] I forgot about the kegs. We used to name our milestones after whiskey, and when we shipped, we would all taste the whiskey. Kevin Gibbs had very good taste in whiskey. He always picked cool ones.

My alcoholism aside, is it an important point? We’re talking on double denim Thursday. Rituals matter to groups of people, whether they’re in business or team sports or any kind of group.

They are. Mihai, who’s out there somewhere, has always been a steward of our traditions. People spend a lot of time at work. They are here because they want to make an impact, and they probably want to make some money, but they also want to enjoy themselves. Especially at a startup. You can say work isn’t a family, but it’s not totally dissimilar from one, in the sense you’re all in this together.

What’s unique about a startup is that, financially, you’re really in it together. Odds are it won’t work, and that happens. But if it does work, your equity is worth more than your salary, almost independent of your title. If you’re in a group of 20, you’re either going to be worth a lot or not. That creates a sense of one and community, and it’s why there’s less politics in startups in a really nice way.

These traditions are part of playing for the front of the jersey rather than the back. Like any other quirky thing, it’s part of being in a community. It’s funny, I still have no idea where double denim came from. We just do it now. And I think that’s the best type of tradition. No one really knows, and everyone’s got five different stories. I’m glad Pinecone couldn’t figure it out.

What do you do outside of Sierra when you have some free time?

I love to cook. That’s probably my favorite hobby outside of technology. Most weekends I’ll cook on both Saturday and Sunday. I feel a sense of loss if I don’t, actually.

What’s your specialty?

On a trip to Italy, I learned how to make pasta. So I make pasta. The kids love it. It’s a crowd pleaser. Otherwise, it’s a mix of typical California stuff: Italian, French, I just like using fresh ingredients. We’re just blessed to have such great produce nearby. So it’s fusion-y type things, but skewed towards Italian because my kids love it.

Not just because you like cooking, but by the time you were 35, you were the elder statesman of tech. You’re now 46. There is no one better qualified to answer this question. Is it harder or easier than ever to build an enduring company? 

I have a theory that I have been tempted to write up but haven’t had the time or rigor required. 

I’m here to help.

Yeah, no, please. It’s the type of thing you probably want to pressure test, but the idea is: The faster your company grows, the more vulnerable it is to competition. 

When I left Google, Google Maps still had less traffic than MapQuest. Anyone with a brain knew Google Maps was going to overtake it, but it hadn’t yet. After I left Google, I remember meeting Matt Cohler, who was still at Facebook. They were looking at a graph of MySpace’s traffic against Facebook’s. In my mind, Facebook had already won, but its line hadn’t passed MySpace’s yet.

The stereotype of network-effect businesses (like social networks) is that they’re more durable, and there are aspects of them that are. But the virality that’s symbiotic with these network effects is also an asset that lets a competitor grow very quickly.

Look at Google versus Facebook. In theory, with search, you can just use a different search page. But Google has had much less competition than Facebook, which has faced Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and others. If you want to start a competitor to search—forget AI, which is a whole different disruptive force, and just think about the traditional search page—how do you grow it? There isn’t any obvious way other than slowly and durably. Because there’s no built-in growth mechanism, it’s actually more durable.

Look at the famous, or infamous, companies that grew quickly, like Clubhouse. The faster you grow, the more likely it is that your growth comes from a mechanism your competitors can use too. When I see the revenue growth in AI, there is an aspect of this. You can see it in coding agents. If you talk to 10 engineers here, they’ll tell you a day they switched from Codex to Claude or vice versa.

The fog of war is probably as thick as it’s ever been, but it has multiple layers. For a start, how durable is your revenue? I can tell you why Sierra’s is, in my opinion. We’ve really been thoughtful about it. But also, the marginal cost of making software is going down with AI. So does that mean it will change the build-versus-buy equation in some structural way? Maybe, but certainly it will increase competition. And in theory, that should reduce profit margins.

So the short answer is, I don’t know and no one knows.

Our philosophy here at Sierra has been to try to be thoughtful about creating durable relationships with our clients, so it’s not transactional. That manifests in a bunch of ways, from how our contracts work to how we engage. We also just plan for—volatility doesn’t quite capture it—an unknown future. The premise, which is very reductive, is that we’ll figure it out if we continue to deliver a lot of value to our customers.

But I couldn’t tell you with a straight face exactly how this is all going to play out. If you’d asked me three years ago what the profit margins of licensing tokens would be versus applied AI, I would have inverted the current margin structure. Now, it’s because there’s a compute shortage and all these other things. How is it going to play out two years from now? I have theories, but it necessitates a lot of agility. It’s probably the most unpredictable time in software that I’ve ever lived in.

Does that make you excited or nervous?

Both, by far. When you’re trying to create a durable company, it causes you anxiety. But in general, when there are brand-new technologies, the pendulum of advantage swings from incumbents to new entrants, because you can be native to that technology. The hardest thing for a startup is all the incumbents. There’s that old adage: No one gets fired for buying IBM. Now that changes, so all of a sudden you at least have a chance.

You mentioned Sierra’s revenue is durable, in your estimation. How much of that is tied to you and your team seeing the whites of your customers’ eyes? The contrast being that one day I can use ChatGPT, the next day I can use Claude. I’ve never spoken to anyone from either business. I feel no guilt when I switch. 

It’s exactly how we think about it.

Even pre-AI, if you looked at the B2B software market and targeted sole proprietors and small businesses, you generally had much higher attrition. Whereas if you sell to the big four banks, they’re much more intentional about their purchasing decisions, and as a consequence, much less likely to change their minds.

When we started Sierra, we thought AI agents as digital front doors would be useful for everybody. But in the short term we thought they’d be more useful for larger businesses, based on the premise that if you have millions of clients, you literally couldn’t afford to talk to them.

I tell this joke a lot, but it’s true.

It would be much easier for me to call Sundar than to reach Google customer support. Google just can’t afford to talk to people. It’s not because they don’t like you. They probably report it publicly, but whatever their average revenue per customer is, it’s less than the cost of a phone call. So they can’t, and that’s true of any business with millions of clients. The ones who can afford to talk to you are, say, the mobile operators, because your lifetime value is higher. But even they aren’t talking to you as much as you’d want, or as much as they’d want.

Our thesis was also that, given the chaos, those would probably be more durable relationships than if we went after small businesses. That’s why we decided to focus on the biggest 2,000 companies in the world. It just felt like the right thing for our business. It requires more of us. You can’t just throw technology over the wall. They expect a higher level of service, but with that comes more durability.

For luddites like me who haven’t seen agents at work, when have you had a “holy shit” moment?

We work with a few different companies that do home loans. In the U.S., there are a bunch of different products. You might be buying a home, or refinancing it. There’s a financial product called a home equity line of credit, where you can essentially get some cash out of your home. We work with Rocket Mortgage, and with some digitally native companies like Figure.

These companies are essentially building digital, I’ll say, loan officers. The agents help you through the process, which, if you’ve ever done it, is quite intimidating. You have to collect all your financial information. You have to get your credit checked. Sometimes you have to get things notarized. The agent is essentially acting as an advocate for you, the borrower.

A lot of people drop out of the process because of how complicated and intimidating it can be. Figure was quite public with some of the metrics they saw from their agent, which I was very grateful for. I think it was converting at 140% of the previous rate. It all comes down to these agents being proactive and infinitely patient.

One of the stories told at Sierra Summit, our customer conference a few weeks ago, came from Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s chief operating officer. He showed how Sierra AI agents onboard couriers and drivers. If you’re familiar with that process, it’s almost like a bank’s KYC [Know Your Customer] process—background checks and things like that. Again, a lot of people start it and don’t finish it. Having an AI agent there to shepherd you through the process is great for everyone. It helps earners navigate the process and become couriers or drivers. And Uber, which competes with a lot of firms for the supply side of its marketplace, is converting at a higher rate too.

The way I like to think about it is this. If you had infinite money and didn’t care about being profitable, you would have a one-to-one account manager for every one of your customers. Every day they would wake up and ask, “What am I going to do today to make you happier?” Maybe spend more with us, whatever it might be. But that’s totally intractable. It just wasn’t financially feasible. Now you can sort of get there.

Think about the term “internet native.” I don’t know when it became popular, but I’d say the early 2000s. It described companies that started digitally first. My sense is that if you start with an AI agent, your customer experience is very different. You almost think of your customers as a segment of one, where every individual has a very unique experience with your product or offerings, whether it’s insurance, a home loan, a retail bank or a retailer. Then you start thinking of an AI agent almost as an individual advocate. It’s a funny, opinionated word, but they’re almost an advocate for the customer. They’re there to represent them as much as they’re there to represent your brand.

This reminds me of vibe coding, which I liken to Instagram. It sounds fantastic but it’s not real, at least for the 99% of us.

I called Sonos last week because I know you work with them. After 15 seconds of fluff about how the EU was going to monitor and record the call, I got the dulcet tones of a Sierra agent. But when I began to ask my question, now 40 seconds into the call, another automated voice, sent from Brussels I presume, cut me off to confirm I was in agreement with their privacy rules. I then got put on hold. So I hung up.

I guess the question is, you can build incredible technology and agents, but how hard is it to implement them in someone else’s business?

This is the ultimate challenge of enterprise software. And also, by the way, success has 1,000 fathers and failure is an orphan. If it’s a great deployment, it’s definitely not because of us. If it’s a bad deployment, it definitely is. That’s just the nature of things.

I actually view that as the bar I try to hold our company to: Can we be proactive enough and trusted enough to help our customers do things the right way? There’s so much behind that. What do you do when the customer’s wrong? Rarely is it an effective strategy to say, “You’re wrong.” Often there’s a very thoughtful person who just might not have the context, or might be misguided for another reason. So how do you develop enough trust, enough data and a deep enough relationship that you can help guide people towards outcomes?

We have a set of company values. The values themselves aren’t particularly novel. Customer obsession is one of them. But Clay and I put a lot of thought into the words after each one. One of the sentences is roughly, “We evaluate ourselves by business outcomes, not technical milestones.” It was designed to capture what you’re talking about. It’s so easy for a tech vendor to say, “We launched. We did it. We got paid,” or whatever it is, and not actually deliver the transformational experience the client was going for.

I think it’s one of our strengths, relatively speaking, though that doesn’t mean we’re perfect at it. We try to embed with our clients and help them with these deployments. That way we can bring together our experience with applied AI, which is fairly unique, with their expertise about their business, their technology and their customers. When we do it well, the whole can be much greater than the sum of its parts. But it is the ultimate challenge for enterprise software.

You’ve been building agents for a long time. Well, a long time in today’s world. Personal agents have had a big coming out party in the last couple of months. Are there any features in the product or the adoption or the marketing that have surprised you?

Yeah, probably the main thing, is how unstructured they are. One of the defining characteristics of these personal agents is that every evening, they sit there and ask, “What should I do for you?” I think they actually use the term “dream.” 

We’ve thought a lot about that. Is it something we should be doing? If you think about most agents powered by businesses, there’s typically a person in charge of the process. Think of onboarding a new client at a bank, or returning an unused item to a retailer. There’s a person whose job is to define the guardrails of that process. But a lot of the delight in using something like Muse or Instinct is the “Hey, I proactively noticed there are weather delays in Denver. There’s another flight with a layover in a different city. Would you like me to rebook you on it to reduce the risk?” You’re like, “Oh man, how cool is that?”

I think of it almost as a question of agent architecture. How open-ended are these experiences? It’s really interesting, and I think it will definitely influence what we and our clients end up wanting to do with company agents as well.

Is the constraint compute? Would it just cost a lot of money to have these things continuously dreaming? Because it seems obvious that you should do it, but I don’t know how this works exactly, so I imagine it’s difficult for other reasons too. 

There are a few things. One is, do you have a channel to proactively engage with the person? Muse is an app; you add Instinct as a contact in your phone. The form factor is designed to be two-way. Some of our clients have agents with a two-way relationship to their customers, and some don’t. It’s actually non-trivial. One of the clever things about Instinct is that there isn’t really an app.

Number two is just how expansive you want these things to be. To some degree, your personal agent has license and permission to be as broad as anything, right? But let’s take, I don’t know, your bank. What guardrails do you want on that agent, and how do you actually express them? What’s interesting about Muse and Instinct is they’re intentionally broad.

There’s this interesting sense of, I don’t know the right word, but authorship. How does the company put its own guardrails around what the agent does? And then how do you, as the consumer, shape it? That’s an evolving conversation, to say the least. As much as I think we should do it, I think you’re right, it’s going to be an interesting design space over time.

With the rise of personal agents, how should companies think about differentiation? Because in the past, a lot of value came down to customer service. But now if I’m just talking to my Muse or my Instinct, I might never interact with the company myself. It doesn’t matter if the place I’m buying from has the sweetest old granny out front or a nightmare-inducing checkout flow. They’ll both be dealing with my agent.

Yeah, I’ll start with my theory on differentiation and then talk about personal agents. They’re related, but there are some nuances. Our theory is roughly what you said. It will be impossible to differentiate with intelligence.

Right now, that’s not true. I think there’s a first-mover advantage. I was too young to remember the first banks that made websites, but it must have been really neat to be able to sign in and check your balance. For that period, if you had AOL or whatever, it might have actually swayed your decision about where to have your checking account.

It’s like Starlink and airlines at the moment.

That’s a great analogy. Right now, you’re like, “I’m going to fly United,” or whatever it is. But at some point, internet will just be great on all airplanes. You assume the technology will dissipate, and it will be the opposite. You have to have an AI agent, or I’m not going to work with you.

At that point, our view is that the differentiator is context, which is essentially the unique data about your interactions with that company. If it’s a big retailer, what have you purchased with them before? What was in your cart at the same time? No matter how advanced AI is, it won’t know that. Then the question is, can you take that context and produce an experience that’s differentiated? I think the answer is yes. In fact, one of the things we promote with our platform is that if your AI agent is your digital front door, every interaction adds to that context.

I’ll give you an example. If you add something to a cart on a website, the company doesn’t know why you made that decision. But if you’re talking to a conversational commerce agent, you might say, “I’m hosting a birthday party for my daughter. Do you have any unicorn candles?” There’s so much context in that question, which the business didn’t get from you adding unicorn candles to a cart. You know it’s a daughter, you know roughly when her birthday is, you know all these things.

So if you have a durable relationship with that customer, maybe next time the birthday comes around, you say, “What are you planning this year? Do you want to get ahead of it? We have some good unicorn stuff.” Or maybe she’s moved on from unicorns. That kind of thing was science fiction before, but it would be quite delightful if done with empathy.

It’s obviously something that digital native companies like Google and Amazon have done really well. Your stuff is there, so you build around it. I actually think companies can do this in general. Those who lean in can end up with this durable moat of context that deepens with every interaction their agent has. And with more intelligence it becomes more useful.

So that’s our theory on differentiation, and we’re trying to help our customers with it, particularly because we work with about half of the Fortune 50. These companies have a lot of customers, and if they get in front of this, they can deepen their competitive moats.
